title: Building a Flashlight That Reveals What the World Already Is
concept_layer: color as the chosen subset of wavelengths offered by a light source; subtractive interaction between colored light and colored surface
domain_deferred: human color perception → later color maps (SimultaneousContrast, MetamerismLab)

capture_leaks.perception_context: Color isn't wavelength — it's what your eye+brain decide. Simultaneous contrast (later in this sequence) breaks the naive model.
capture_leaks.metamerism: Different wavelength mixes can look identical to us; MetamerismLab addresses this.
capture_leaks.subpixel_rendering: The flashlight projects 'pure' colors but your screen reconstructs them from three subpixels. A whole world of approximation lives here.
capture_leaks.material_response: A surface doesn't have 'a color' — it has a spectral response function. This map uses Godot's simplified albedo model; the full story waits.

limit: A flashlight with a single exported color seems simple. Under it, three assumptions: that color is one vector in RGB, that surfaces respond linearly, that seeing is objective. Every one of those is wrong in interesting ways. The next maps in this sequence begin dismantling them.

stages.title: From rotation to quality
stages.thinking: Trans_Rotation taught you that orientation lives on a curved manifold and Euler angles are a leaky chart. Now a new kind of property: not where a form is, not which way it faces, but what it *is like*. Color is the first quality. Geometry has said nothing about this until now — a point has position, a line has length, a triangle has area, but none of them have hue. Color is where mathematics meets perception.
stages.code:
# Previous sequences:
#   primitives — where (position, extent, closure)
#   transformation — how (translate, rotate, scale)
#
# New question: what is a form LIKE?
#
# In Godot, color is a Color — four floats (r, g, b, a)
# Each in [0, 1]. Together they represent the simplest
# additive model of how humans see light.

@export var light_color: Color = Color.WHITE

# This is the seed. Everything else follows from it.

stages.title: Light is directed, not ambient
stages.thinking: The first tool the player gets for working with color is a flashlight — a SpotLight3D. This is deliberate. Ambient light fills space uniformly; the world has a color all the time. A flashlight only colors what it hits. This teaches color as an *interaction* between a source and a surface, not a property hanging in the air.

stages.title: Walk the tree to find the light
stages.thinking: This script attaches to a flashlight model. It needs to find the SpotLight3D buried inside. Recursion walks the node tree. A pattern that reappears everywhere: a script configures a feature buried in a scene by descending and matching a type. First example of dynamic scene traversal in the curriculum.

stages.title: Tint the lens so the color is visible even when off-target
stages.thinking: A colored flashlight shining on a wall colors the wall. But what about the flashlight itself? A white flashlight emitting red light should LOOK red — its lens should glow. We find the lens mesh by name and apply a material with emission matching the light. This is where color stops being a number and starts being a seen thing.

stages.title: See the subtractive truth
stages.thinking: Here's where the lesson lands. The flashlight emits red light. You shine it on a blue wall. The wall goes nearly black. Why? Because the blue wall reflects blue wavelengths; the red flashlight offers no blue to reflect. Color is not additive on surfaces — it is the intersection of what the light offers and what the surface reflects. White flashlights hide this because white contains everything.
stages.code:
# The player slides a color into the flashlight
# and points it at a wall. What happens?
#
# red flashlight on blue wall   → nearly black
# red flashlight on red wall    → bright red  
# red flashlight on white wall  → red (white reflects all)
# red flashlight on yellow wall → red (yellow = red + green)
# green flashlight on yellow    → green (same reason)
#
# Color on a surface is an AND gate:
# what the light offers  AND  what the surface reflects.
# No shared wavelength → darkness.

# This is why the flashlight matters.
# A white flashlight would hide the truth.
# A colored flashlight reveals what the world is made of.

stages.title: Unambiguous choice: one color, one identity
stages.thinking: No animation, no cycling, no slider. The flashlight's color is set once in _ready() and never changes. Why this restraint? Because this map is about understanding one fixed color's interaction with many surfaces. Swapping between flashlights (done at the map level, not the artifact level) is the ritual. Each flashlight IS its color.

stages.title: Works whether attached to flashlight, parent, or target path
stages.thinking: The target resolution is flexible because flashlights get placed in maps in different ways — sometimes this script attaches to the flashlight root, sometimes to a sibling, sometimes via explicit NodePath. Three fallbacks. This kind of flexibility is invisible when it works, invaluable when it fails elsewhere.

stages.title: Give it identity
stages.thinking: A flashlight knows what it is. Not an object that adds color to the world — a device that chooses which wavelengths to offer. The world's color was always there. The flashlight reveals it by editing what it gives. This is color as relation, not color as attribute. The whole Color sequence unfolds from this.
stages.code:
# @identity
# essence: SpotLight3D.light_color = exported color — tints a flashlight beam and its lens mesh to match
# desire: to hold a colored flashlight in VR and paint the world with tinted light, seeing how surfaces respond to non-white illumination
# critical_parameter: light_color — the single color that defines everything: beam hue, lens tint, and emission glow
# triggers: _ready applies color once; no runtime changes — the flashlight's color is its identity
# emerges: colored light on colored surfaces creates unexpected results (red light on blue wall = black) teaching subtractive interaction
# needs: SpotLight3D [has]; lens mesh tinting [has]; VR grab [missing]; color picker [missing]
# relationships: synthesis artifact for Color_Flashlight map; contrasts with ambient-light artifacts
# truth: a flashlight does not add color to the world — it reveals what was always there by choosing which wavelengths to offer
